name: Andrew Jackson vetoes the Second Bank of the United States
scope: The pre-Fed showdown that killed America's first attempt at a permanent central bank. T1: the SECOND BANK OF THE UNITED STATES, chartered in 1816 for a 20-year term, was a privately-owned bank with a federal monopoly to issue banknotes and hold Treasury deposits -- run by NICHOLAS BIDDLE of Philadelphia from 1823. T2: President ANDREW JACKSON, elected 1828, believed the Bank concentrated financial power in a handful of eastern financiers and foreign shareholders (roughly a quarter of the stock was held in Britain). He made killing the Bank the defining fight of his presidency. T3: on JULY 10 1832, Jackson VETOED the bill to recharter the Bank -- one of the most famous vetoes in American history. His veto message called the Bank a threat to democracy, arguing that Congress could not grant monopoly privileges that made 'the rich richer and the potent more powerful.' T4: the confrontation is remembered as the BANK WAR. Biddle tried to force Jackson's hand by deliberately CONTRACTING credit to trigger a recession and blame Jackson (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Biddle's role in the 1833-34 credit contraction is documented in his own letters). Jackson's response was to WITHDRAW federal deposits from the Bank and place them in state-chartered 'pet banks.' T5: Jackson is reported to have declared to a Bank delegation: 'YOU ARE A DEN OF VIPERS AND THIEVES. I INTEND TO ROUT YOU OUT, AND BY THE ETERNAL GOD, I WILL ROUT YOU OUT!' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: this quote is traditionally attributed but the primary source is contested -- present as attributed). The Bank's federal charter lapsed in 1836; the United States would have no central bank again for 77 years. Further rungs: Jackson survived an ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT in January 1835 by Richard Lawrence, whose two pistols both misfired -- Jackson later blamed the Bank's supporters; the political party formed to oppose Jackson was called the WHIGS, casting Jackson as 'King Andrew.'
source: PRIMARY: Andrew Jackson's Veto Message of July 10 1832 (available in the Presidential Papers); Nicholas Biddle correspondence 1833-34. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Second Bank of the United States', 'Bank War', 'Andrew Jackson' (2026-09-05) -- 1816 charter, Biddle presidency from 1823, July 10 1832 veto date, deposit withdrawal 1833, 'pet banks', charter lapse 1836, the Lawrence assassination attempt January 30 1835. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact veto date; the 'den of vipers' quote's primary source (traditionally attributed to Jackson's confrontation with a Bank delegation, but historians disagree on which meeting and exact wording); the extent of foreign ownership of Bank stock.
framing_note: The founding-generation American CRITIQUE of central banking, told as a personality-driven fight so kids meet Jackson before they meet the Fed. Dinner-test payoff: T5 (a sitting president said 'you are a den of vipers and thieves' to bankers in his own office and won). SCENE-LED: never 'what was the Second Bank?' -- always the July 10 1832 veto, the Bank War, the withdrawal of deposits, the vipers quote. BASTIAT PATTERN check: this is an INCENTIVE RECOGNITION anchor -- Jackson SAW the incentive a chartered monopoly creates (rent-seeking, capture by wealthy shareholders, foreign influence over domestic credit). Not yet ABCT, but the concentrated-benefit / dispersed-cost move Olson would later formalize. ACCURACY RAIL: the 'den of vipers' quote is TRADITIONALLY attributed but its exact wording and precise setting are contested by historians -- present it as 'reportedly said' or 'traditionally quoted', never as verbatim documentary evidence. Biddle's deliberate credit contraction of 1833-34 IS well-documented in his own letters. RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT: the stem does not have to say the Bank was BAD -- it presents Jackson's ARGUMENT (concentrated privilege, foreign ownership) and asks what he DID or what he SAID. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem describes the scene (the 1832 veto, the Bank War, the deposit withdrawal) and the answer is a NAMED THING (Nicholas Biddle, July 10 1832, 'den of vipers', pet banks, the Whig party). DISTRACTOR MINE: other Jackson-era figures (Henry Clay who championed the Bank, John C. Calhoun, Martin Van Buren), other presidential vetoes (Cleveland's pension vetoes, Truman's Taft-Hartley veto), other 'first-central-bank' fights (Alexander Hamilton vs Jefferson over the FIRST Bank in 1791). The assassination attempt is a HISTORY fact that becomes economics only through Jackson's own linkage of it to Bank supporters.

name: The free-banking era and the National Banking Acts
scope: The 77 years between the Second Bank and the Fed. T1: after Jackson killed the Second Bank in 1836, the United States entered what economists call the FREE BANKING ERA (roughly 1837-1863). Individual states passed 'free banking' laws letting anyone who met capital requirements charter a bank and issue their own banknotes backed by bonds on deposit with the state. T2: at the peak, hundreds of DIFFERENT PRIVATE BANKNOTES circulated at once. Merchants used printed 'banknote reporters' to check which notes were sound and at what discount they traded. Notes from a distant, unfamiliar bank might trade at 90 cents on the dollar; notes from a failed bank at zero. T3: contrary to popular textbook accounts, RECENT SCHOLARSHIP (Rolnick + Weber, Federal Reserve Bank of Minneapolis 1983; CORROBORATE AT BUILD) has shown the free-banking era was NOT the chaos it is often painted as. Bank failure rates and noteholder losses in the well-regulated free-banking states (New York, Massachusetts) were modest -- comparable to bank losses in the later, more regulated eras. T4: during the CIVIL WAR, Salmon P. Chase's Treasury pushed through the NATIONAL BANKING ACTS of 1863 and 1864, creating federally-chartered 'national banks' that could issue a UNIFORM national currency backed by US government bonds. In 1865, Congress placed a 10% TAX on state banknotes -- effectively taxing them out of existence and forcing banks into the national system. T5: the National Banking system helped FINANCE THE UNION WAR EFFORT (banks were required to hold Treasury bonds as reserves against their note issue -- a captive market for government debt). It centralized note issue but left NO LENDER OF LAST RESORT for panics -- which meant that every major panic (1873, 1893, 1907) had to be handled by ad-hoc private rescues. That gap became the political case for creating the Federal Reserve. Further rungs: the term 'wildcat bank' comes from the 1830s-40s Michigan and Indiana banks that placed their redemption offices in remote wooded locations where wildcats supposedly outnumbered noteholders; the greenback dollar (fiat notes issued by the Union to pay for the war) is a separate story from national bank notes.
source: PRIMARY: National Bank Act of 1863 (12 Stat 665); National Bank Act of 1864 (13 Stat 99); the 1865 Revenue Act imposing the 10% tax on state banknotes. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Free banking era', 'National Banking Acts of 1863 and 1864', 'Wildcat banking' (2026-09-05); Rolnick + Weber, 'New Evidence on the Free Banking Era' (American Economic Review 1983, from Minneapolis Fed research). CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact citation and findings of Rolnick + Weber 1983; the wildcat-bank etymology (traditional but colorful, sometimes disputed).
framing_note: The historical bridge between Jackson and Jekyll Island -- shows the kid that America ran WITHOUT a central bank for a lifetime, with mixed but not catastrophic results. Dinner-test payoff: T2 (hundreds of different banknotes at once, with printed guides telling you which ones to trust) and T3 (the free-banking era was NOT the chaos textbooks claim -- modern research corrected the story). SCENE-LED: 'For 77 years America had no central bank. Merchants carried printed guides to tell them which of the hundreds of private banknotes were sound.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: this is a KNOWLEDGE-PROBLEM anchor in reverse -- decentralized noteholders solved the trust problem through DISCOUNT PRICING and reputation, an emergent-order solution the standard textbook narrative obscures. Also a moral-hazard preview -- without a lender of last resort, banks had to be more careful because no one would bail them out. ACCURACY RAIL: Rolnick + Weber's revisionist findings are the modern consensus but not universally accepted; frame as 'recent scholarship shows' rather than 'proved.' The 'wildcat bank' etymology is traditional but colorful. RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT: this is a historical-institutional ladder, no policy verdict imposed. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: stem gives the scene (private notes, banknote reporters, the National Banking Acts, the 10% tax) and the answer is a NAMED THING (1863-64, Salmon P. Chase, 10% tax on state notes, no lender of last resort). DISTRACTOR MINE: other Civil War financial measures (the greenback dollar 1862, the Legal Tender Acts, war bond drives), other pre-Fed central-banking systems (Bank of England 1694, Reichsbank 1876), other Treasury Secretaries (Alexander Hamilton, Andrew Mellon).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the Civil War as war and Salmon P. Chase as a political figure (Chief Justice, presidential candidate); economics owns the National Banking Acts as MONETARY institutions and their fiscal-war-finance function.

name: The Panic of 1907 and J.P. Morgan's private rescue
scope: The panic that became the political argument for creating the Fed. T1: in OCTOBER 1907, a failed attempt by copper-market speculators Otto and Augustus Heinze to corner the market in United Copper Company crashed. When their scheme failed, depositors began pulling money from banks associated with them, and the run spread. T2: the KNICKERBOCKER TRUST COMPANY, the third-largest trust in New York, was drained in a matter of days after its president Charles Barney was linked to the Heinze scheme. It suspended withdrawals on OCTOBER 22 1907. Panic spread across Wall Street. T3: with NO CENTRAL BANK to act as lender of last resort, the private banker J.P. MORGAN, then 70 years old, organized the rescue himself. He summoned the presidents of the major trust companies and national banks to his personal LIBRARY at 219 Madison Avenue and LOCKED THEM IN, refusing to let them leave until they had committed pooled funds to stop the runs (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the 'locked in the library' detail is well-attested by Satterlee's Morgan biography). T4: Morgan personally led the coordination for weeks. When the New York Stock Exchange threatened to close due to lack of liquidity, Morgan told its president Ransom Thomas that closing 'would be too great a shock' and produced $25 million from bank presidents in his library within 15 minutes. He also organized the rescue of Trust Company of America, which he judged solvent, and let Knickerbocker fail. T5: the panic became the POLITICAL ARGUMENT for a permanent central lender-of-last-resort. Senator Nelson Aldrich chaired the NATIONAL MONETARY COMMISSION (1908-1912) to design a solution. Morgan-allied bankers concluded that leaving future panic responses to one aging private banker was not a repeatable strategy. Within three years, they would gather at Jekyll Island to draft what became the Federal Reserve Act. Further rungs: the Panic of 1907 is sometimes called the KNICKERBOCKER CRISIS after its most prominent failure; Treasury Secretary George Cortelyou deposited $35M in national banks to help; historian Charles Kindleberger called Morgan's rescue 'the last time an individual acted as a central bank in a major crisis.'

CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Panic of 1907', 'Knickerbocker Trust Company', 'J. P. Morgan', 'National Monetary Commission' (2026-09-05) -- Heinze copper corner October 1907, Knickerbocker suspension October 22 1907, Morgan's library rescue, the $25M NYSE rescue, Cortelyou's $35M Treasury deposit, Aldrich commission 1908-12. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact date of the Knickerbocker suspension; the 'locked in the library' detail (well-attested but embellished in some retellings); the precise $25M NYSE figure.
framing_note: The lever event -- kids see the political ARGUMENT for a central bank being made in real time. Dinner-test payoff: T3 (one old private banker LOCKED his rivals in his personal library and would not let them leave until they wrote checks) and T4 ($25 million raised in 15 minutes from men in a library). SCENE-LED: 'October 1907. A copper-market corner has just collapsed. Runs are spreading. There is no central bank.' BASTIAT PATTERN check: this is an INCENTIVE RECOGNITION setup for the Jekyll Island ladder that follows -- the panic created the political demand; the SEEN is 'we need a lender of last resort'; the UNSEEN is 'a permanent one will be captured by the same private bankers who ran the rescue.' RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT: the stem does not judge whether the Fed was the right answer -- it shows the sequence of events that led to the argument for one. ACCURACY RAIL: Morgan's central role is not disputed by any serious historian; the detail level (which bankers, which trust companies) is well-documented. The Kindleberger quote is real. Do NOT paint Morgan as a hero or a villain; he was an ACTOR with his own interests in the outcome. name: Jekyll Island: the secret meeting that drafted the Fed
scope: The private meeting on a Georgia island that produced the blueprint for the Federal Reserve. T1: in NOVEMBER 1910, six men boarded Senator NELSON ALDRICH'S private railcar in New Jersey, told to bring hunting clothes and to use only first names in front of servants. They travelled south to the JEKYLL ISLAND CLUB, a private hunting retreat off the coast of Georgia owned by a small group of America's richest families. T2: the six were: NELSON ALDRICH (Republican senator from Rhode Island, father-in-law of John D. Rockefeller Jr.); PAUL WARBURG (Kuhn, Loeb & Company partner, German-born banking-family expert on European central banks); FRANK VANDERLIP (president of National City Bank of New York, the Rockefeller bank); HENRY DAVISON (senior partner at J.P. Morgan & Co.); BENJAMIN STRONG (Bankers Trust president, later the first NY Fed governor); and A. PIATT ANDREW (Assistant Treasury Secretary). T3: for roughly ten days they worked in secret to draft what became the ALDRICH PLAN -- the blueprint for a private-public central banking system. The men SWORE SECRECY. Vanderlip did not publicly acknowledge the meeting until an article in the Saturday Evening Post in FEBRUARY 1935 -- twenty-five years later. T4: the Aldrich Plan, presented as Senator Aldrich's Republican bill, was politically dead because of Aldrich's association with Wall Street. But when the Democrats took Congress in 1912 and Wilson took the White House, the SAME BASIC STRUCTURE (regional banks, note-issue power, private-bank ownership of regional-bank stock) was passed under Democratic sponsorship as the FEDERAL RESERVE ACT, with mostly cosmetic changes. T5: the men who drafted the Fed were the very men whose banks and financial dynasties would benefit from the institution's structure. Vanderlip later admitted: 'There was an occasion, near the close of 1910, when I was as secretive -- indeed as furtive -- as any conspirator... I do not feel it is any exaggeration to speak of our secret expedition to Jekyll Island as the occasion of the actual conception of what eventually became the Federal Reserve System.' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: Vanderlip's 1935 Saturday Evening Post article, 'From Farm Boy to Financier'). Further rungs: G. Edward Griffin's 1994 book 'The Creature from Jekyll Island' popularized the meeting for a mass audience; the club building where they met still stands and is preserved as a historic site.

name: The Federal Reserve Act of December 23, 1913
scope: The law that created the Federal Reserve System. T1: the FEDERAL RESERVE ACT was signed into law by President WOODROW WILSON on DECEMBER 23 1913 -- two days before Christmas, after most members of Congress had already left Washington for the holidays. T2: the Act created a system of TWELVE regional Federal Reserve Banks (Boston, New York, Philadelphia, Cleveland, Richmond, Atlanta, Chicago, St. Louis, Minneapolis, Kansas City, Dallas, San Francisco) overseen by a FEDERAL RESERVE BOARD in Washington. The regional banks were owned by their member commercial banks, not by the government. T3: the Act gave the Fed the power to ISSUE FEDERAL RESERVE NOTES (the paper currency you carry today), to hold member-bank reserves, to lend to member banks at a DISCOUNT RATE, and to conduct OPEN MARKET OPERATIONS (buying and selling Treasury securities to expand or contract the money supply). T4: the underlying structure -- regional banks, private ownership, note-issue power -- was substantively the ALDRICH PLAN drafted at Jekyll Island in November 1910. The Democratic version rebranded it as public-friendly (calling the regional banks 'Federal Reserve Banks' rather than 'National Reserve Association branches') but kept the essential mechanism designed by Warburg. Congressman Charles Lindbergh Sr. (father of the aviator) warned during debate: 'This Act establishes the most gigantic trust on earth... The invisible government by the money power will be legalized' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: date and exact wording of Lindbergh Sr's congressional statement). T5: WILSON is often reported to have said, near the end of his life: 'I HAVE UNWITTINGLY RUINED MY COUNTRY. A great industrial nation is controlled by its system of credit... we have come to be one of the worst ruled, one of the most completely controlled and dominated governments in the civilized world.' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: this quote is DISPUTED -- the second half about 'controlled and dominated' is from Wilson's 1913 book 'The New Freedom,' pre-signing; the 'I have unwittingly ruined my country' portion has no verified primary source and is likely apocryphal. Present as ATTRIBUTED-BUT-DISPUTED.) Further rungs: Wilson had campaigned for the presidency partly on trust-busting and financial reform; Senator Robert Owen (D-OK) was the Senate sponsor and Representative Carter Glass (D-VA) the House sponsor of the final version.

name: Benjamin Strong and the coup de whiskey of 1927
scope: The first powerful Fed chief and the rate cut Rothbard blamed for the 1929 crash. T1: BENJAMIN STRONG had been at the Jekyll Island meeting in 1910 as president of Bankers Trust. When the Fed opened for business in 1914, he became the FIRST GOVERNOR of the FEDERAL RESERVE BANK OF NEW YORK -- the most powerful of the twelve regional banks because it sat in the financial capital. T2: the Federal Reserve Act had not clearly designated who would be the system's leading voice: the Washington Board or the New York bank. In practice, from 1914 until his death in 1928, Strong ran Fed policy. He built the NEW YORK FED into the system's operational center and pioneered OPEN MARKET OPERATIONS (buying Treasury securities to inject reserves into the banking system) as a policy tool. T3: Strong developed a close personal friendship with MONTAGU NORMAN, Governor of the BANK OF ENGLAND from 1920 to 1944. Britain, having returned to the gold standard at pre-war parity in 1925, was struggling with an overvalued pound. Strong agreed to help by keeping US interest rates LOW -- to reduce the incentive for gold to flow FROM Britain TO the United States. T4: in JULY 1927, Strong hosted Norman, France's Emile Moreau, and Germany's Hjalmar Schacht at a secret meeting on Long Island. Days later the Fed cut its DISCOUNT RATE from 4% to 3.5%. Strong reportedly described the cut privately as 'a little COUP DE WHISKEY to the stock market' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the 'coup de whiskey' phrase is attributed to Strong via Adolph Miller's later Senate testimony -- present as attributed). T5: MURRAY ROTHBARD, in 'America's Great Depression' (1963), argued that this 1927 rate cut was the DECISIVE ACT of monetary expansion that fueled the final malinvestment phase of the 1920s boom -- the malinvestment that would collapse in October 1929. From an Austrian perspective, Strong's death in October 1928 removed the one Fed official who might have known when to stop; the following year the boom he inflated broke. Further rungs: Strong had tuberculosis for years and died at 55; the M2 money supply grew roughly 60% from 1921 to 1929, most of it during and after the 1927 easing; Adolph Miller was the dissenting Fed Board member who later blamed Strong publicly.

name: The 1929 crash: Black Thursday and Black Tuesday
scope: The stock-market panic that ended the Roaring Twenties. T1: the ROARING TWENTIES saw the DOW JONES INDUSTRIAL AVERAGE rise from about 63 in August 1921 to a peak of 381 on SEPTEMBER 3 1929 -- roughly a six-fold gain in eight years, fueled by easy credit, margin buying (investors could buy stock with 10% down), and the widespread belief that stocks only went up. T2: the crash came in two waves. On BLACK THURSDAY, OCTOBER 24 1929, panicked selling gripped the New York Stock Exchange; leading bankers pooled money for a rescue (echoing 1907 but on a larger scale) and briefly stabilized prices. T3: five days later, on BLACK TUESDAY, OCTOBER 29 1929, the market broke completely. Roughly 16 million shares traded (a volume record that stood for decades), and the Dow fell nearly 12% in one day. Margin calls forced cascading liquidation. T4: the Dow continued to fall for nearly three years, bottoming at 41.22 on JULY 8 1932 -- an 89% peak-to-trough decline. It would not regain the September 1929 peak until 1954. T5: the CRUCIAL AUSTRIAN AND MONETARIST POINT: the 1929 crash was a SYMPTOM, not the cause of the Great Depression. Recessions had followed stock-market crashes before (1907, 1920-21) without becoming decade-long depressions. What TURNED the crash into a decade of misery was the Fed's failure to prevent the money supply from collapsing by 33% over the next four years and the government's tariff, tax, and wage-policy interventions. The crash tested the SYSTEM; the SYSTEM failed the test. Further rungs: Yale economist Irving Fisher famously said on October 15 1929 that stocks had reached 'what looks like a permanently high plateau' and lost his personal fortune in the crash; the 1920-21 depression (see separate ladder) is the counterfactual case where the Fed did NOTHING and the recession ended within 18 months.

name: Friedman and Schwartz: the Great Depression as monetary failure
scope: The 1963 book that established the modern consensus on what caused the Great Depression. T1: in 1963 the economists MILTON FRIEDMAN and ANNA SCHWARTZ published 'A MONETARY HISTORY OF THE UNITED STATES, 1867-1960,' an 860-page study of American monetary events across a century -- a book so influential that Ben Bernanke would later call it 'the leading and most persuasive explanation of the worst economic disaster in American history.' T2: Chapter 7, 'THE GREAT CONTRACTION 1929-1933,' presented the case that the Great Depression was fundamentally a MONETARY FAILURE. The M2 money supply CONTRACTED by roughly 33% between 1929 and 1933 -- a collapse the Fed had the tools to prevent and did not. T3: between 1930 and 1933 approximately 9,000 US BANKS FAILED (out of roughly 25,000 in operation in 1929). Each failure destroyed the deposits held there (there was no FDIC until 1933), further contracting the money supply. The Fed, chartered specifically to be the lender of last resort, mostly stood aside as regional banking systems collapsed. T4: Friedman and Schwartz argued that the failure had specific institutional causes: Benjamin Strong's death in 1928 left the Fed without a dominant policymaker; the Federal Reserve Board was fragmented and paralyzed; the DOCTRINE that the Fed should not 'bail out' banks it judged unsound became a suicide pact for the entire banking system. T5: on NOVEMBER 8 2002, at a conference honoring Friedman's 90th birthday, then-Fed Governor BEN BERNANKE gave a speech that concluded: 'Let me end my talk by abusing slightly my status as an official representative of the Federal Reserve. I would like to say to Milton and Anna: Regarding the Great Depression -- YOU'RE RIGHT. WE DID IT. WE'RE VERY SORRY. But thanks to you, we won't do it again.' (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact speech text, Federal Reserve archive). The Austrian critique (Rothbard) went further -- the 1920s expansion Friedman + Schwartz downplayed was itself the seed of the crash. But the CORE POINT -- the Fed's contraction 1929-33 caused the Depression -- became mainstream. Further rungs: Anna Schwartz continued working into her 90s and died in 2012 at age 96; the book was published by the National Bureau of Economic Research (Princeton University Press); Friedman won the Nobel Prize in 1976, Schwartz never did despite co-authoring the definitive American monetary history.

name: Smoot-Hawley Tariff and the collapse of world trade
scope: The tariff act that turned a US recession into a global depression. T1: on JUNE 17 1930, President Herbert Hoover signed the SMOOT-HAWLEY TARIFF ACT (formally the Tariff Act of 1930) sponsored by Senator Reed Smoot (R-UT) and Representative Willis Hawley (R-OR). T4: BASTIAT'S REASONING (a century earlier, in France) had already exposed what Smoot-Hawley would do: the SEEN was protection for domestic producers of specific goods; the UNSEEN was (a) higher prices to American consumers, (b) foreign markets closed to American exports, (c) the loss of the specialized-production gains that trade creates. name: FDR's gold seizure: Executive Order 6102 and the 1934 devaluation
scope: The confiscation of American gold and the 77% devaluation of the dollar's savers. T1: on APRIL 5 1933, five weeks after his inauguration, President FRANKLIN D. ROOSEVELT signed EXECUTIVE ORDER 6102, requiring all US citizens to TURN IN their gold coins, gold bullion, and gold certificates to the Federal Reserve by MAY 1 1933, in exchange for paper Federal Reserve Notes at a fixed rate of $20.67 per troy ounce. T2: the penalty for refusing to turn in gold was severe -- a fine of up to $10,000 (roughly $240,000 in 2026 dollars) and up to 10 YEARS in prison. Citizens were permitted to keep small amounts (up to $100 face value in gold coins and coins of recognized numismatic value), but bulk holdings were confiscated. T3: the ORDER was issued under authority of the TRADING WITH THE ENEMY ACT of 1917 (a wartime law) as amended by the Emergency Banking Act of March 9 1933. In effect, the US government treated its own citizens as if they were foreign belligerents in wartime for the purpose of seizing gold. T4: on JANUARY 30 1934, the GOLD RESERVE ACT was signed, and on JANUARY 31 1934 Roosevelt issued a proclamation raising the official gold price from $20.67 to $35.00 per ounce. The dollar was DEVALUED BY 40.94% against gold. Anyone who had turned in gold coins the previous year at $20.67 could NOT buy them back at $35.00 -- the government kept the difference. This was an implicit ROUGHLY 77% DEVALUATION of the purchasing power of savers who had held gold (a $20.67 dollar bought only 59% of what a $35 gold ounce did). T5: the SEEN was 'strengthening the banking system by preventing gold hoarding.' The UNSEEN was that AMERICAN SAVERS -- disproportionately the middle-class households who had prudently held gold as a store of value -- were transferred wealth to the US Treasury via the devaluation. Roosevelt's gold order was upheld by the Supreme Court in the 1935 GOLD CLAUSE CASES (5-4), which also declared unconstitutional the government's abrogation of gold-clause obligations in its own bonds but held that bondholders were not entitled to damages. The prohibition on private gold ownership REMAINED IN FORCE until December 31 1974, when Congress repealed it under President Gerald Ford. Further rungs: numismatic and 'rare coin' collections were exempt -- which created a workaround (some Americans bought old gold coins at premiums to legally hold gold); the Fort Knox Bullion Depository was built in 1936 specifically to house the seized gold.

name: Fed-Treasury Accord and William McChesney Martin's punchbowl
scope: The 1951 restoration of Fed independence and the era's longest-serving chair. T1: during WORLD WAR II and after, the Fed had agreed to PEG US Treasury bond prices at levels the Treasury wanted -- effectively financing the war effort by keeping government borrowing costs artificially low. T2: on MARCH 4 1951, the Fed and the Treasury announced the FEDERAL RESERVE-TREASURY ACCORD, restoring the Fed's independence to set monetary policy without pegging Treasury bond prices. Historians consider this the moment the modern independent Fed was born -- 38 years after the Federal Reserve Act. T3: shortly after the Accord, President Harry Truman appointed WILLIAM MCCHESNEY MARTIN JR. as Fed CHAIRMAN in April 1951. Martin had actually helped NEGOTIATE the Accord from the TREASURY side, but Truman appointed him hoping he would prove loyal. Truman is reported to have said later that Martin 'double-crossed' him. T4: Martin served as Fed chairman for NEARLY 19 YEARS (April 1951 to January 1970) under presidents Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, Johnson, and Nixon -- the LONGEST-SERVING Fed chair in history. He believed the Fed's job was to LEAN AGAINST inflationary pressures from Washington, resisting political pressure to keep rates low. T5: in an OCTOBER 19 1955 SPEECH to the New York Group of the Investment Bankers Association of America, Martin used the metaphor that made his career: the Fed's role was to be 'the chaperone who has ordered the punch bowl removed just when the party was really warming up.' The 'TAKE AWAY THE PUNCHBOWL' metaphor became the classic description of anti-inflationary central banking -- the Fed's job is to be UNPOPULAR precisely when the boom feels best. Further rungs: Martin's father WILLIAM MCCHESNEY MARTIN SR. had been the first governor of the FEDERAL RESERVE BANK OF ST. LOUIS -- one of very few father-son central bankers in US history; Martin faced increasing pressure from LBJ's Great Society spending in the mid-1960s and eventually gave in to some inflationary policy, contributing to the setup for the 1970s inflation.

name: The Nixon shock: August 15, 1971 and the birth of pure fiat
scope: The Sunday-night broadcast that ended dollar-gold convertibility and began the pure-fiat era. T1: on SUNDAY, AUGUST 15 1971, President RICHARD NIXON preempted the popular television show 'BONANZA' with a NATIONAL BROADCAST from the Oval Office announcing sweeping economic measures. The centerpiece: the United States would SUSPEND CONVERTIBILITY of the dollar into gold for foreign central banks. T2: this was known immediately as the NIXON SHOCK. It formally ENDED the BRETTON WOODS SYSTEM that had governed global money since 1944, and inaugurated the era of PURE FIAT CURRENCY -- money backed by nothing but government promise. As of 2026, no major national currency has been convertible to any commodity for over 54 years. T3: Nixon's announcement was actually a PACKAGE of three measures: (1) 'closing the GOLD WINDOW' -- suspending foreign-central-bank gold convertibility; (2) a 90-day WAGE AND PRICE FREEZE, the first peacetime price controls in US history; (3) a 10% IMPORT SURCHARGE to punish trading partners perceived to be manipulating their currencies. Nixon's Treasury Secretary JOHN CONNALLY reportedly told a European finance-ministers meeting: 'The dollar is our currency, but it's your problem.' T4: the timing was DOMESTIC POLITICAL. Nixon faced re-election in November 1972. His advisers (including Fed Chairman Arthur Burns) worried a gold-drain crisis would force austerity that would hurt Nixon at the polls. Closing the gold window unilaterally shifted the pain to foreign holders of dollars. The wage-price freeze bought a temporary appearance of inflation control until after the election. Nixon won 49 states in 1972; the underlying inflation exploded in 1973-74. T5: from an AUSTRIAN perspective, the Nixon shock was the CULMINATION of a decade of fiscal recklessness (Great Society + Vietnam) that Bretton Woods could not accommodate. From a BITCOIN-perspective, August 15 1971 is the FOUNDING DATE of the political-money problem that Satoshi's white paper would try to solve 37 years later -- a currency untethered from any physical anchor, whose value depends entirely on the political promise of central banks. The website WTFHAPPENEDIN1971.COM documents dozens of economic indicators (wage-productivity divergence, household savings, wealth concentration) that visibly change trend around 1971. Further rungs: Nixon aide William Safire, who witnessed the Camp David planning weekend where the decision was made, called it 'the most important act of Nixon's presidency other than opening China'; John Connally became a Republican after starting as a Texas Democrat and briefly ran for president in 1980.

name: Arthur Burns, Nixon's political pressure, and the 1970s Great Inflation
scope: The Fed chairman who caved and the inflation that followed. T1: after Nixon appointed him Fed CHAIRMAN in FEBRUARY 1970, ARTHUR BURNS (Columbia economics professor, former head of the National Bureau of Economic Research) inherited an economy already carrying inflationary pressure from the 1960s Great Society + Vietnam War spending. T2: NIXON PRESSURED BURNS to keep interest rates LOW ahead of the November 1972 election. The NIXON TAPES (recorded in the Oval Office and later released as part of the Watergate investigations) preserved Nixon telling aides that Burns had to be kept 'IN LINE' and Burns being pressured directly. Burns's OWN DIARIES (published 2010 as 'Inside the Nixon Administration: The Secret Diary of Arthur Burns 1969-1974') documented the pressure and Burns's private discomfort. T3: Burns COMPLIED. The Fed kept monetary policy LOOSE through 1971-72. Combined with Nixon's wage-price freeze (August 1971) creating pent-up price pressures, and with the OPEC oil embargo of OCTOBER 1973 sending oil prices from $3 to $12 per barrel, the mid-1970s saw inflation accelerate: 1974 CPI 11.0%, 1979 CPI 11.3%, 1980 CPI 13.5%. T4: STAGFLATION -- the combination of high inflation AND high unemployment -- was supposed to be IMPOSSIBLE under the reigning Keynesian PHILLIPS CURVE model, which predicted inflation and unemployment as trading against each other. MILTON FRIEDMAN, in his 1968 American Economic Association presidential address, had predicted exactly stagflation would occur if the Fed kept trying to buy lower unemployment with higher inflation -- because workers would come to EXPECT the inflation, and the trade-off would break. The 1970s proved Friedman right and mainstream Keynesianism spectacularly wrong. T5: the AUSTRIAN critique was even sharper. name: The Phillips curve's death and Friedman's 1968 vindication
scope: The Keynesian model that stagflation destroyed. T1: in 1958, LSE economist A.W. PHILLIPS published a paper showing a HISTORICAL CORRELATION in British data between UNEMPLOYMENT and WAGE INFLATION -- when unemployment was low, wages rose fast; when unemployment was high, wages rose slowly. This became the PHILLIPS CURVE. T2: through the 1960s, mainstream Keynesian economists interpreted the Phillips curve as a permanent POLICY TRADEOFF -- if you were willing to accept HIGHER INFLATION, you could BUY LOWER UNEMPLOYMENT (and vice versa). This became the theoretical justification for expansionary monetary and fiscal policy: 'a little more inflation for a little less unemployment.' T3: in his AMERICAN ECONOMIC ASSOCIATION presidential address of DECEMBER 1967 (published in the American Economic Review March 1968), MILTON FRIEDMAN attacked the Phillips curve directly. His argument: workers are NOT FOOLED FOREVER. Once inflation becomes EXPECTED, workers demand wage increases to compensate. The trade-off between inflation and unemployment is TEMPORARY -- once expectations adjust, the same unemployment rate coexists with any inflation rate. There is a 'NATURAL RATE OF UNEMPLOYMENT' that monetary policy cannot change. T4: EDMUND PHELPS made a similar argument independently the same year (later winning the 2006 Nobel Prize for this work). Friedman and Phelps predicted: if the Fed persistently tried to buy lower unemployment with higher inflation, the result would be BOTH higher inflation AND unemployment eventually returning to natural rate -- STAGFLATION, which the standard Phillips curve said was impossible. T5: the 1970s DELIVERED EXACTLY THIS. Unemployment in the US averaged 6.2% for the decade (up from 4.8% in the 1960s) while inflation averaged 7.1% (up from 2.5% in the 1960s). By 1979 the US was experiencing SIMULTANEOUS 6% unemployment AND 11% inflation. The standard Keynesian textbook Phillips curve was FALSIFIED. Friedman won the Nobel Prize in 1976 partly for this prediction. From an AUSTRIAN perspective, Friedman was correct as far as he went but the deeper Austrian point was that the ATTEMPT to fine-tune the economy by expanding credit ALWAYS eventually produces the same result. Further rungs: the 'EXPECTATIONS-AUGMENTED PHILLIPS CURVE' that survived the 1970s falsification is now standard in macroeconomics textbooks; A.W. Phillips himself was an inventor and engineer before becoming an economist -- his MONIAC hydraulic computer built in 1949 simulated the British economy using water flowing through pipes.

name: The Fed's dual mandate and the Austrian critique
scope: The 1978 law that set the Fed's incompatible goals. T1: for most of its history, the Fed's mandate was ambiguous -- the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 spoke vaguely of 'furnishing an elastic currency' without setting specific goals. This changed with the HUMPHREY-HAWKINS FULL EMPLOYMENT AND BALANCED GROWTH ACT of 1978 (also called the Humphrey-Hawkins Act after its Senate and House sponsors HUBERT HUMPHREY (D-MN) and AUGUSTUS HAWKINS (D-CA)). T2: the Act established the Fed's DUAL MANDATE -- to conduct monetary policy to achieve (1) MAXIMUM EMPLOYMENT and (2) STABLE PRICES. A third goal, 'moderate long-term interest rates,' is technically also mandated but is treated as derivative. T3: the Act was passed in the LATE 1970S -- during the very period when the Phillips curve was being FALSIFIED by stagflation. It embedded into US law the very trade-off assumption (that the Fed could pursue BOTH goals) that Friedman + Phelps had just shown to be theoretically unsustainable in the long run. T4: the AUSTRIAN CRITIQUE (Mises, Rothbard, and modern Austrians): the two goals are IRRECONCILABLE. Maximum employment above the natural rate REQUIRES persistent monetary expansion; monetary expansion PRODUCES inflation. In practice, the Fed CHOOSES between the mandates in every rate decision, and the political incentive is always to LEAN toward the employment side (because unemployment is politically salient in a way that inflation is not until it becomes severe). T5: the AUSTRIAN prediction: over any long period, a Fed with a dual mandate will produce BOTH persistent low-grade inflation AND asset bubbles -- because the employment mandate provides political cover for keeping money loose, and the price-stability mandate is measured on CONSUMER PRICES only, leaving asset-price inflation (housing, stocks) uncounted. The 1990s dot-com bubble, the 2000s housing bubble, and the 2020s asset-price boom all fit this pattern. The 2020-22 inflation event, in which the Fed initially called the price surge 'TRANSITORY' and only tightened after clear failure, was for Austrians the definitive vindication -- the employment-side bias produced predictable inflation error. Further rungs: Hubert Humphrey died a year before the Act passed -- it was named in his honor by his surviving co-sponsors; other central banks (the European Central Bank, the Bundesbank before it) have a SINGLE PRICE-STABILITY mandate specifically to avoid the dual-mandate problem; Milton Friedman had long advocated a purely rule-based monetary framework (constant money-supply growth) precisely to remove Fed discretion over the trade-off.

name: Continental Illinois 1984 and the birth of too-big-to-fail
scope: The bank rescue that established the modern moral-hazard doctrine. T1: CONTINENTAL ILLINOIS NATIONAL BANK, based in Chicago, was in 1984 the SEVENTH-LARGEST US bank by assets. Conover told Congress on SEPTEMBER 19 1984 that federal regulators would protect the 11 largest US banks against failure, effectively announcing a formal 'TOO BIG TO FAIL' policy (CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact congressional testimony citation). name: The Latin American debt crisis and Brady bonds

T2: on AUGUST 12 1982, MEXICO's Finance Minister JESUS SILVA HERZOG informed the US Treasury that Mexico could no longer service its foreign debt. The Brady Plan is now considered the successful RESOLUTION mechanism -- but the AUSTRIAN critique notes that (a) the workout socialized the losses through prolonged Latin American suffering rather than immediate bank failure, and (b) the workout entrenched the pattern of IMF/Fed coordination to protect major banks that would recur in every subsequent international debt episode. Further rungs: Walter Wriston's 'countries don't go bankrupt' quote from 1982 became the emblematic banker-hubris quote of the era; Argentina, Brazil, and Mexico had cumulative INFLATION rates in the hundreds or thousands of percent during the 1980s; Mexico's per-capita GDP in constant dollars did not regain 1981 levels until the mid-1990s.

name: Greenspan takes over and Black Monday 1987
scope: The Fed transition and the first modern flash crash. T1: on AUGUST 11 1987, President Ronald Reagan appointed ALAN GREENSPAN as Federal Reserve Chairman, succeeding Paul Volcker. name: Long-Term Capital Management and the 1998 rescue

name: The FOMC: who actually decides US monetary policy
scope: The specific committee that sets the Fed funds rate. T1: the FEDERAL OPEN MARKET COMMITTEE (FOMC) is the group that actually decides US monetary policy. Its DECISIONS -- to raise, lower, or hold the FED FUNDS RATE, and to buy or sell Treasury securities -- are the operative acts of the Federal Reserve System. T2: the FOMC has TWELVE VOTING MEMBERS at any meeting: the SEVEN MEMBERS of the FEDERAL RESERVE BOARD OF GOVERNORS in Washington (nominated by the President, confirmed by the Senate for 14-year terms), plus FIVE OF THE TWELVE REGIONAL FEDERAL RESERVE BANK PRESIDENTS. T3: crucially, the PRESIDENT OF THE FEDERAL RESERVE BANK OF NEW YORK holds a PERMANENT voting seat on the FOMC -- the only regional president with an always-vote. The other 11 regional presidents rotate through the remaining four voting seats on annual cycles. This structure gives the NY Fed (which conducts the actual open-market operations for the whole system) outsized influence, dating back to the 1913 founding when it was the largest bank district. T4: the FOMC MEETS EIGHT times per year, roughly every 6-8 weeks. Each meeting produces a POLICY STATEMENT (announcing the target Fed funds rate and any policy changes), and DETAILED MINUTES released three weeks later. The Fed Chair holds a press conference after each meeting. Chair PATTERN since 1979: Volcker, Greenspan, Bernanke, Yellen, Powell -- each one has had disproportionate agenda-setting influence within the committee. T5: the AUSTRIAN + PUBLIC-CHOICE critique: the FOMC is a small, unelected committee making decisions of enormous consequence for the value of the currency held by ~330 million Americans (and, via reserve-currency status, billions of non-Americans). Its members are drawn heavily from academic economists (Bernanke, Yellen, Powell all had academic or regulatory backgrounds) and from the banking industry (regional presidents typically come from bank supervision or trading backgrounds). The COMMITTEE has no direct democratic accountability -- Board members' 14-year terms are the longest of any US government body except the Supreme Court; regional presidents are not confirmed by the Senate at all. From an Austrian perspective, no committee -- no matter how well-intentioned or credentialed -- can possess the DISPERSED KNOWLEDGE required to set 'the correct' interest rate for an economy of hundreds of millions of participants (Hayek's knowledge problem, applied to central banking). Further rungs: the FOMC's meeting statement wording is scrutinized so intensely that specific word changes (e.g., 'appropriate' vs 'patient') can move markets by billions of dollars; the Chair's press-conference performance has been called 'more market-moving than the actual policy decision'; the term 'Fed watcher' names an entire subprofession of analysts who parse FOMC output.
